tier_reason: The thesis PDF in the repo compares RadixSIMD against STLSort, which src/sort_methods.hpp (SortMethodSTLSort) implements as std::sort with std::less, driven by src/perf-thesis.cpp. It states gcc 12.1.0 and an Intel Core i7-12700K at 5 GHz (section 7.4), and the Makefile gives -std=c++20 -O3 plus the AVX-512 flags, so code, compiler, flags and CPU model are all public.

corrections.caveats: Bachelor's thesis benchmark (not peer reviewed) with the author's own harness (src/perf-thesis.cpp with src/sort_methods.hpp; results written to /tmp). STLSort is std::sort over DataElement structs with std::less; libstdc++ is implied by gcc 12.1.0 on Manjaro, not stated. The Makefile was edited after the thesis (commit 'Add warnings in Makefile', 2023-12-15), so the thesis-time flags are inferred from the current file. Timing uses CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID, averaged over max(1, 2^18/n) runs after warmup runs. The perf harness only checks sortedness (a separate test program checks keys and payloads). The cross-algorithm comparison covers only 2^18 elements. Not faster everywhere: in appendix B RadixSIMD is slower than std::sort in 19 of 56 key/distribution cases, including sorted, reverse-sorted and almost-sorted inputs for int32, int32-int32, float, float-int32 and double, and Zero/ZeroOne inputs with payloads or double keys (for example double Zero 14.37 vs 4.77 ns/element and int32 ReverseSorted 5.56 vs 3.02 ns/element). It is also slower than IPPRadix, BramasSort and BlacherSort on the headline cases; the thesis says most of its time is spent in the comparison sorter. The README says a quicksort variant performed about the same and was not published as a paper, and points to Intel x86-simd-sort as an equally generic alternative. AVX-512 is required (the i7-12700K had it enabled in the BIOS). The IPP rows need the proprietary Intel IPP library.

notes: The headline numbers in Figures 8.16, 8.17 and 8.18 match the thesis exactly (10.16 vs 41.87, 11.19 vs 41.94 and 16.33 vs 44.71 ns/element). Shortcoming to record: RadixSIMD loses to std::sort on presorted and reverse-sorted inputs and on several constant-key cases (19 of 56 appendix B cases), and on the headline cases it is slower than IPP, Bramas and Blacher sorts. MIT, 15 stars, last commit 2025-01-31 (stale), and not already listed (the catalog lists x86-simd-sort, vxsort and berenger-eu/avx-512-sort separately).

tier_reason: The README states the 4-6x figure over the scalar PQ Scan reference and cites the peer-reviewed PVLDB 9(4) paper. Search snippets confirm that the paper reports a 4-6x reduction in scan latency, but the paper itself was not opened here (vldb.org DNS blocked, snippet only). No CPU model is on any reachable page, so the record cannot reach A even though the code (pqfastscan) and flags (CMakeLists) are public.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'PQ Fast Scan to perform 4-6x faster than PQ Scan, while returning the exact same results' (chart image not readable here). The README's sample pqfastscan output gives pq_us 75392 vs fast_pq_us 12272 (about 6.1x) and 74754 vs 17480 (about 4.3x) for two queries on a partition of 25,159,451 codes (derived from page data). PVLDB paper: 4-6x lower scan latency (search snippet only; the paper could not be opened).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ 4.9.x ('we benchmarked it with this version only'); CMakeLists.txt: -std=c++11 -g -ggdb -O3 -m64 -march=native -ffast-math -Wall -Werror, AVX option ON, AVX2 option OFF
corrections.caveats: Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed PVLDB 9(4) paper (Andre, Kermarrec, Le Scouarnec; presented at VLDB 2016). The paper could not be opened (vldb.org blocked), so the 4-6x figure comes from the README and a search snippet. No reachable page gives a CPU model. The baseline is the authors' own scalar PQ Scan. In the README's pqscan output the SSE+prefetch (91214) and AVX+vgather+prefetch (97841) variants are slower than the scalar scan (74758), while AVX+prefetch (68490) is about 9% faster, so most of the gain comes from the register-resident lookup tables, not from vectorizing the plain scan. Builds use -march=native -ffast-math. The technique requires reorganizing the code lists (grouping), which the Quick ADC README says prevents combining it with inverted indexes, and it was tuned for 8x8-bit PQ codes on ANN_SIFT100M1 partitions. The datasets were generated with a commercially licensed libpq. Clear BSD has no patent grant and is not OSI-listed (permissive, treated as copyable).
corrections.workload: Nearest-neighbour scan of 8x8-bit product-quantized codes (ANN_SIFT100M1 split into 8 partitions of about 25M codes, ANN_SIFT1B queries): the distance lookup tables are kept in SIMD registers instead of the L1 cache and the results are exactly the same as PQ Scan.

notes: The README matches the claim and the sample output rows support 4.3x to 6.1x (derived). Tier B rests on the PVLDB paper, which is known only from search snippets. Shortcomings to record: no CPU model on reachable pages, the authors' own scalar baseline, -march=native -ffast-math, and a code layout that cannot be combined with inverted indexes. 70 stars, 15 forks, last commit 2019-05-31 (abandoned). Not a duplicate, though Faiss (wave 8) later adopted a related 4-bit fast-scan approach (from memory, not checked here).

tier_reason: The README claims 4-6x over the scalar ADC reference, shows one example run (scan 86 us vs 323 us) and cites the peer-reviewed ICMR 2017 paper. The paper (arXiv 1704.07355, ACM) could not be opened here; its abstract says 3 to 6 times (search snippet only). No CPU model is given for the numbers, so the record stays below A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'Quick ADC achieves 4-6x better performance than ADC by storing lookup tables in SIMD registers'. The README example on SIFT1M with an IVF index of 256 cells and ma=24 gives scan_us 86 for db_query_4 (16x4 OPQ, Recall@100 0.9426) vs 323 for db_query ADC (8x8 OPQ, Recall@100 0.9646), about 3.8x (derived from page data). Paper abstract (arXiv 1704.07355): a 3 to 6 times speedup over ADC (search snippet only).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ 5.4 or newer; CMakeLists.txt: -std=c++14 -g -O3 -m64 -march=native -ffast-math -fopenmp -Wall -Werror; sequential (single-threaded) BLAS, OpenCV core, Cereal 1.2.2
corrections.caveats: Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed ICMR 2017 paper cited in the README; the paper (ACM and arXiv) could not be opened here, so the figures come from the README and a search snippet (the abstract says 3-6x, the README 4-6x). The README example compares different quantizers (16x4 OPQ for Quick ADC vs 8x8 OPQ for ADC) at lower recall (0.9426 vs 0.9646), and Quick ADC scans a 'keep' fraction of codes without SIMD first, so the 3.8x example is not like for like. 4-bit quantizers cost some accuracy (the README calls it slight and often negligible). The baseline ADC is the authors' own scalar implementation. Tested on Intel Haswell, Broadwell and Skylake, but no CPU model is given for the published numbers. Builds use -march=native -ffast-math. Clear BSD has no patent grant and is not OSI-listed (permissive, treated as copyable).

notes: The README matches the 4-6x claim. The reachable example gives about 3.8x (derived) at lower recall with a different quantizer, and the paper abstract says 3-6x (snippet only). Shortcomings to record: not like for like (16x4 vs 8x8 codes, lower recall), the authors' own baseline, no CPU model, and the paper not opened. 27 stars, 3 commits, last commit 2019-05-31 (abandoned). Sibling of PQ Fast Scan (same authors, different technique), not a duplicate.
